ModMetadata.Name: IZCode
ModMetadata.Author: julianobd
ModMetadata.Description:
IZCode replaces IC10 with IZ: a structured programming language with types, real functions and recursion, running on its own virtual machine inside the Programmable Chip.
Write '#iz' on the first line of a chip and the mod takes over. Chips without the marker keep working as plain IC10, so nothing you already built changes.
===================================================================== WHY IT EXISTS =====================================================================
IC10 gives you 128 lines, 16 registers you juggle by hand, and a program that restarts from the top on every tick. IZ gives you named variables, functions with parameters and return values, and a VM that freezes its complete state when the tick budget runs out and resumes at the very next instruction.
That last point is the big one: an infinite loop does not freeze the chip.
IC10 IZ ---- -- 128 lines bounded only by the source size 16 registers, managed by hand named variables, allocated by the compiler jal/ra, one practical level fn with parameters, returns and recursion restarts every tick the VM freezes and resumes where it stopped an infinite loop hangs the chip preempted by budget, the game carries on typos found at runtime compile errors, with a name suggestion everything is a double num, bool, str, dev checked at compile time HASH("x"), the text is gone a real str: joined, compared, hashed at runtime 16 loose registers struct and arrays, in a real heap
===================================================================== A COMPLETE PROGRAM =====================================================================
#iz device sensor = d0; device inlet = d1; device outlet = d2;
const TARGET = 101.325; const MARGIN = 5.0;
fn main() { loop { var p = sensor.Pressure;
inlet.On = p < TARGET - MARGIN; outlet.On = p > TARGET + MARGIN;
yield; } }
Execution starts at fn main(). When main returns, the chip stops until it is restarted.
===================================================================== TYPES =====================================================================
num 64-bit floating point (IEEE-754). The one numeric type. bool true / false str ASCII text, immutable, built and compared while the program runs dev device handle (pin d0-d5) T[N] array of exactly N values of type T struct a group of named fields, declared by your program
There are no separate integers: as in IC10, everything is num. Bitwise operations convert to a 64-bit integer, operate, and convert back.
num and bool are NOT implicitly interchangeable. 'if x' requires a bool; write 'if x != 0'. That removes IC10's biggest source of silent bugs. The conversion in the other direction IS allowed, so 'pump.On = p < 100' works as written.
===================================================================== VARIABLES AND CONSTANTS =====================================================================
var counter = 0; // inferred: num, mutable var active: bool = false; // explicit annotation const MAX = 101.325; // constant, folded at compile time
const only accepts expressions computable at compile time, and costs nothing at runtime: the value is folded into every use.
Variables declared outside a function are globals and keep their value across function calls and across ticks.
===================================================================== ARRAYS AND STRUCTS =====================================================================
Everything above fits in one number. An array or a struct does not, so it lives in the VM heap and the variable holds its address. The whole layout is decided at compile time: there is no allocator to call and nothing to collect.
var samples: num[8]; // eight cells, zeroed var levels = [10, 20, 30]; // inferred: num[3]
samples[0] = sensor.Pressure; samples[1] += 5;
The length is part of the type and has to be known at compile time, so it is a literal or a const, never a variable. num[3] and num[4] are different types. len(a) answers the length and is folded into a constant, so it costs nothing:
for i in 0..len(samples) { total += samples[i]; }
Dimensions read left to right, as in C: num[2][3] is 2 groups of 3.
A struct groups what belongs together, and is declared outside any function:
struct Gauge { total: num; cursor: num; samples: num[8]; }
var a: Gauge; a.samples[3] = 12;
A field holds the value, not a reference to it, so the layout stays flat and a struct cannot contain itself. Two structs with the same fields are still different types: what matches is the declaration, not the shape.
Arrays and structs travel by reference, which is why a function fills one in instead of handing it back:
fn fill(xs: num[3]) { xs[1] = 42; } // the caller sees the 42
The cells belong to the call that declared them and are released when it returns. So a recursive call gets its own array, a declaration inside a loop hands back the same cells cleared again instead of leaking, and a global keeps its values across ticks. For the same reason a function cannot RETURN an array or a struct, and an aggregate variable is bound once, at its declaration: both rules exist so an address can never outlive the memory behind it.
An index outside the array stops the chip with a runtime error - and when the index is a constant, the compiler catches it before you ever press CONFIRM.
===================================================================== DEVICES =====================================================================
device pump = d0; // housing pin device sensor = d1;
Reading and writing use property access, validated at compile time against the game's LogicType table:
var p = sensor.Pressure; // error if the property does not exist pump.On = true; // error if it is read-only
Slots work the same way:
var q = chute.slot[0].Quantity;
A typo in a property name is caught at compile time, and the message suggests the closest real name:
'Presure' is not a known device property; did you mean 'Pressure'?
===================================================================== HASH LITERALS AND BATCH OPERATIONS =====================================================================
The housing has only six pins. A batch operation reaches any number of devices on the same data network, identified by the prefab hash - no cable needed to each one.
all(StructureWallLight).On = true; // every device of that prefab named("Corridor Light").On = false; // any prefab, by label named(StructureVolumePump, "north").On = true; // prefab AND label
A batch read aggregates by average. If nothing matches the filter, the result is 0.
var average = all(StructureGasSensor).Pressure;
The prefab can be written three ways, all producing the same constant at compile time (zero runtime cost):
all(StructureWallLight) bare name all(#"StructureWallLight") hash literal const LIGHT = #"StructureWallLight"; all(LIGHT) constant
RESOLUTION RULE: a bare identifier counts as a prefab name only if nothing is declared with that name. If a const, var or parameter with that name exists, its value is used instead.
Prefer the constant when the same prefab appears more than once. A typo in the name produces a perfectly valid hash that matches nothing and fails silently; declaring it once keeps the mistake in a single place.
The 'named' label written as a literal or a const also becomes a hash at compile time, so it can live in a constant and be passed as a parameter:
const NORTH = #"north";
fn turn_off(wing: num) { named(StructureVolumePump, wing).On = false; }
A label or a prefab whose text is only known while the program runs is hashed then, by the same CRC32 - see TEXT below.
===================================================================== TEXT =====================================================================
In IC10 a piece of text only ever became a number: HASH("name") at compile time, and the text itself was gone. In IZ a str is a value like any other. It goes in a variable, a parameter, a return, an array cell or a struct field, and it can be built while the program runs.
var side = "north"; var label = "vent-" + side; // "vent-north"
if label == "vent-north" { ... }
+ and += join two str; they never mix with a num == != compare the text, not the storage < <= > >= ordinal order, so "B" comes before "a"
A number gets in through text(x), which is deliberate: silently turning 42 into "42" inside a '+' is how a typo becomes a label nobody notices.
A const may hold text, and two of them join at compile time:
const SIDE = "north"; const LABEL = SIDE + "-wing"; // folded; free at runtime
WHAT TEXT REACHES THE WORLD THROUGH. The game's logic network carries numbers only, so a device property and a batch write still refuse a str. What connects the two is the hash:
all("Structure" + kind).On = true; // hashed while it runs named("vent-" + side).On = true; var h = hash("StructureWallLight"); // same value as #"StructureWallLight"
hash() of a literal or of a str const is folded at compile time, so everything that was free before str became a value is still free.
MEMORY. Text built at runtime lives in a table of 512 slots, each up to 256 characters. The same text always lands on the same slot, so a loop rebuilding "tag-" + suffix every tick allocates once and not once per tick; and when the table fills, the VM collects what nobody points at any more. A program that really does hold more than 512 distinct strings at once stops with a runtime error instead of growing without a bound.
len(s) characters hash(s) the CRC32 all() and named() use char(s, i) ASCII code at i, -1 outside the string chr(code) one character from its code sub(s, start, count) both bounds clamped find(s, needle) where it starts, -1 when absent text(x) a num as text fixed(x, decimals) a num as text with a fixed number of decimals parse(s) text back into a num, nan when it is not one
===================================================================== CONTROL FLOW =====================================================================
if cond { ... } else if other { ... } else { ... }
while cond { ... }
loop { ... } // infinite loop
for i in 0..10 { ... } // 0 inclusive, 10 exclusive for i in 0..=10 { ... } // 10 inclusive
break; continue;
There is no goto and there are no jump labels. Parentheses around the condition are optional; the braces are mandatory, which removes the dangling-else.
The 'for' range limit is evaluated exactly once, so changing it inside the body cannot turn the loop into an accidental infinite one.
===================================================================== FUNCTIONS =====================================================================
fn clamp_to(x: num, lo: num, hi: num) -> num { if x < lo { return lo; } if x > hi { return hi; } return x; }
fn warn() { // no return value beacon.On = true; }
A function may call another one declared further down the file. Recursion is allowed and bounded by the call depth limit; overflowing it raises a runtime error instead of corrupting anything.
fn gcd(a: num, b: num) -> num { if b == 0 { return a; } return gcd(b, a % b); }
===================================================================== OPERATORS =====================================================================
From weakest to strongest precedence, all left associative:
|| logical or, short circuit && logical and, short circuit == != < <= > >= | bitwise or ^ bitwise xor & bitwise and << >> shifts + - * / % -x !x ~x prefix a.b a[i] f(x) postfix
'%' takes the sign of the divisor, as in IC10 - not the C# behaviour. Division by zero follows IEEE-754 (inf / nan), it is not a runtime error.
Assignment is a STATEMENT, not an expression: 'if (a = b)' does not compile, which turns the classic C mistake into a clear message.
Compound assignment works on variables and on device properties alike:
x += 1; pump.Setting *= 2;
===================================================================== TICK CONTROL =====================================================================
The chip runs a fixed instruction budget per game tick. There are two ways to hand the tick back:
yield; gives the tick back immediately; resumes at the next instruction sleep(2); suspends for N seconds, then resumes
And a third that costs you nothing to write: when the budget runs out, the VM preempts itself. 'loop { ... yield; }' is the idiomatic main loop, but a loop without yield is simply preempted and keeps running.
===================================================================== BUILT-IN FUNCTIONS =====================================================================
abs ceil floor round trunc sqrt exp log sin cos tan asin acos atan atan2 min max pow sign clamp len(array) the declared length of an array rand() a value in [0,1) nan() inf() isnan(x)
len hash char chr sub find text fixed parse over text
===================================================================== IN-GAME EDITOR TOOLS =====================================================================
Writing '#iz' also upgrades the code editor itself.
A REAL CODE AREA. The Stationeers editor is 128 independent text fields, one per line - which is why you cannot drag a selection across three lines or press Ctrl+A on the whole program. In IZ mode it becomes a single multi-line field with a dark background, a line-number gutter and a current-line highlight, and all of that becomes native: drag selection, Shift+arrows, double click, Ctrl+A/C/X/V, PageUp/PageDown and the mouse wheel.
AUTOMATIC INDENTATION, VS Code style:
Enter repeats the line's indent, goes in one level after '{' Enter between { and } opens both lines with the caret in between } on a blank line goes back one level to line up with the opening brace Tab / Shift+Tab shifts the whole selected block
COMPLETION THAT KNOWS YOUR WIRING. The editor knows which CircuitHousing is selected, and the housing knows what is wired to each pin. Typing 'pump.' suggests the properties of THAT pump, with the live value alongside, instead of all 358 in the game:
pump. On rw Setting rw = 45 Pressure r = 101.325
It also completes pins (device x = shows what is on each one), prefab names inside all(...) and #"...", slot properties, and the names declared in your own program.
Tab accept the suggestion Ctrl + arrows move through the list Ctrl + Space open the full list Esc close it
COMPILE ERRORS WHILE YOU TYPE. The same compiler the chip runs on CONFIRM compiles what is on screen, a fraction of a second after the last keystroke. Problem lines get an underline - red for errors, amber for warnings - and a panel at the bottom says what is wrong:
error line 5 a batch write takes num (or bool), not str warning line 2 const 'LED' was declared and never used
HOVER WITH REAL VALUES. Point at a device variable and see the equipment, its label, its hash and the current value of every readable property. Point at a property and it tells you whether that device accepts it and whether it is read only. Point at a #"..." and it shows the hash, and warns you when no prefab with that name exists.
SYNTAX HIGHLIGHTING built for IZ, in the editor and on the Programmable Chip Motherboard screen - including #"Prefab", which the IC10 highlighter used to swallow as a comment.
===================================================================== ERRORS AND WARNINGS =====================================================================
Compile errors carry the line, the column and the source snippet, and stop the program from ever running. Runtime errors stop the chip and light the housing's error LED, exactly like an IC10 exception.
Warnings do not stop anything. Today there is one: a name declared and never used, which applies to var, const and device - but not to function parameters nor to a for index. Warnings go quiet when the compilation already has an error, since a name may look unused only because the code that would use it is what fails to compile.
===================================================================== CONSOLE COMMANDS =====================================================================
izcode_devices load or build the device catalog and print a summary izcode_devices rescan force a fresh scan (needed after installing a mod that adds devices, since that does not change the game version)
izcode_log show the current log state izcode_log off switch logging off izcode_log level debug talk more izcode_log areas completion,editor only these subjects izcode_log path where the log and the config file are
Files live in Documents\My Games\Stationeers\izcode\ - the device catalog (devices.txt and devices.json), the log (izcode.log) and its configuration (log.cfg).
===================================================================== REQUIREMENTS =====================================================================
IZCode is a C# plugin, and Stationeers does not load C# on its own. Install these first:
1. BepInEx the loader 2. StationeersLaunchPad which runs on top of BepInEx and starts the mod
With both in place, enable IZCode in the mods menu. To confirm it loaded, look for [IZCode] in Player.log - the startup banner comes out even with logging switched off.
===================================================================== SAFE TO TRY =====================================================================
Chips without the '#iz' marker behave exactly as they always did. And because '#iz' starts with '#', which the IC10 parser reads as a comment, a chip carrying IZ code does not break the game for someone who does not have the mod installed.
Example programs ship with the mod, in the samples/ folder: pressure control, solar tracking, batch operations by hash and by label, a moving average, an LED status panel, a rolling window built from a struct and an array, labels built from text while the program runs, recursion, and a full hardsuit systems controller.
